title: Data Warehouse Fundamentals
summary: A warehouse isn't just a bigger database — it's architected around a different question entirely: scanning millions of rows fast, not looking up one row instantly. That difference shapes everything else in this group.

slides.markdown:
An OLTP database is optimized to find and update *one row* fast — a user's profile, a single order. A data **warehouse** is optimized to scan and aggregate *millions of rows* fast — total revenue last quarter, average session length across a billion sessions. Those are different problems, and a warehouse's entire architecture follows from taking the second one seriously.

This topic covers the two architectural pillars that make that possible — massively parallel processing and columnar storage — plus the storage/compute separation that defines modern cloud warehouses, and the pricing and latency expectations that follow directly from all of it.

slides.sectionTitle: MPP: spreading a query across many nodes
slides.markdown:
**Massively parallel processing (MPP)** splits a single query across many worker nodes, each scanning its own slice of the data simultaneously, then combines their partial results into one answer. A query that would take one machine an hour to scan can take a 50-node cluster roughly a minute, because each node is only responsible for 1/50th of the data.

This is fundamentally different from how a single-node OLTP database executes a query — there's no "spread this across 50 machines" step, because OLTP workloads are typically small, targeted lookups where parallelizing wouldn't help. MPP only pays off when a query genuinely has to touch a large fraction of a large dataset, which describes most analytical aggregations and almost no OLTP point lookups.

The practical consequence: a warehouse query's speed scales with how many nodes you throw at it, up to the point where coordination overhead between nodes starts to dominate — which is exactly why warehouse compute is provisioned in clusters, not single machines.

slides.sectionTitle: A query fanning out and re-aggregating
slides.markdown:
Picture a single incoming query — "total revenue by region, last quarter" — hitting a coordinator node, which splits the underlying data by worker and sends each worker the same query logic against its own slice. Each worker computes a partial sum for the regions in its slice; the coordinator then merges those partial sums into the final answer.

![MPP query coordinator scattering work to worker nodes and gathering partial results](assets/mpp-scatter-gather.svg)

slides.markdown:
Warehouses store data **column-by-column** rather than row-by-row: all values for one column sit together on disk, rather than each row's full set of columns sitting together. For a query like `SELECT SUM(revenue)` over a 50-column table, a columnar layout reads only the `revenue` column's bytes — a small fraction of the table — while a row-oriented layout has to read every column of every row just to get at the one it needs.

This is *the* single biggest reason warehouses are fast at aggregation: analytical queries almost always touch a handful of columns across many rows, which is exactly the access pattern columnar storage is built for. Columnar Storage Internals, later in this group, goes into how compression and predicate pushdown build on top of this same layout to cut scan cost further.

OLTP databases default to row storage instead, because their workload — read or write one complete row at a time — is the opposite access pattern columnar layout is optimized for.

Older warehouses bundled storage and compute into one fixed cluster — more storage meant provisioning more machines, whether or not you needed more compute power, and vice versa. Modern cloud warehouses **separate** the two: data sits in cheap, durable object storage, and compute clusters attach to it independently, scaling up or down (or to zero) without moving or duplicating the underlying data.

This decoupling is what makes two things possible that a bundled architecture can't: running multiple differently-sized compute clusters against the *same* data simultaneously (one team's heavy batch job doesn't compete for resources with another team's dashboard queries), and paying for compute only while a query is actually running, rather than for an always-on cluster sized for peak load.

The cost of separation is the network hop between storage and compute on every query — a genuinely bundled system can be faster for a workload that fits entirely in one fixed cluster's local disks, which is part of why some workloads still choose a fixed-cluster model, covered in the Warehouse Platforms Compared topic later in this group.

slides.sectionTitle: Why warehouses scale and charge differently
slides.markdown:
An OLTP database is typically sized for a steady stream of small, concurrent transactions and priced (or provisioned) for that steady load. A warehouse's workload is bursty by nature — most analytical queries run in short, intense bursts (a dashboard refresh, a nightly batch job) with idle time between them — so warehouse pricing models are built around that shape: many charge per query or per second of actual compute used, or let a cluster auto-suspend when idle and auto-resume on the next query.

This is also why a warehouse bill can look alarming if a query scans far more data than it needs to — most consumption-based pricing charges proportional to bytes scanned or compute-seconds used, so an unnecessarily broad scan (covered as a pitfall in the Warehouse Cost & Performance topic later in this group) directly inflates cost in a way a fixed-price OLTP instance never would.

The mental model to carry: an OLTP database's cost is mostly about *provisioning for steady load*; a warehouse's cost is mostly about *how much data your queries actually touch*.

A team builds a user-facing feature — "show this one customer's latest order" — directly against the warehouse, because the data's already there, and is confused when a query that should be instant takes a full second or more.

That latency isn't a misconfiguration; it's the architecture working as designed. A warehouse's whole value proposition is scanning large volumes efficiently via MPP and columnar layout — neither of those techniques accelerates a single-row point lookup, and the coordination overhead of fanning a query out across a cluster can actually make a trivial single-row query *slower* than it would be on a purpose-built OLTP database with an index.

The fix is architectural, not a tuning knob: point lookups belong on an OLTP database (or a fast key-value cache) sized for that access pattern; the warehouse is for the aggregations and scans it's actually built for. Reaching for the warehouse because "the data's already there" is a common and costly shortcut.

slides.sectionTitle: The single source of truth for analytics
slides.markdown:
Beyond its architecture, a warehouse plays a specific organizational role: it's typically the place where data from many different source systems — the OLTP application database, third-party SaaS tools, event streams — gets consolidated into one queryable, governed home for analytics.

This matters because without that consolidation, "what was our revenue last month" can get three different answers depending on which system someone queries — the application database's live numbers, a marketing tool's own tracking, a finance spreadsheet's manual export. A warehouse that's actually treated as the single source of truth means every team building a report or dashboard queries the *same* underlying, reconciled numbers.

That role is a governance and process commitment as much as a technical one — a warehouse can technically hold consolidated data and still fail at being a source of truth if teams keep bypassing it with their own exports and spreadsheets.

slides.sectionTitle: Rough numbers on the scale difference
slides.markdown:
To make MPP's payoff concrete: scanning a 10-billion-row table on a single machine at a few hundred million rows/second might take on the order of 30-60 seconds. Spread that same scan across a 40-node MPP cluster, and each node handles roughly 250 million rows — comparable per-node work to a much smaller single-machine scan — bringing wall-clock time down toward 1-2 seconds, before accounting for coordination overhead.

That overhead is real and grows with cluster size: at some point, adding more nodes yields diminishing returns because the time spent coordinating and merging partial results starts to rival the time saved by parallelizing further. Warehouses handling genuinely massive scans (hundreds of billions of rows) invest heavily in minimizing that coordination cost, which is part of why the specific query-execution engine, not just "more nodes," differentiates warehouse platforms at that scale — covered in Warehouse Platforms Compared.

The number to internalize: MPP's win is real and roughly linear with node count up to a point, not an unlimited multiplier.

This topic covered *why* a warehouse is architected the way it is. The rest of the group goes deeper on each piece: Columnar Storage Internals unpacks exactly how column-oriented layout, compression, and predicate pushdown make scans cheap; Partitioning & Clustering covers organizing data physically so queries scan even less of it; and Warehouse Cost & Performance Optimization covers the levers for controlling what you actually pay once the architecture is in place.

Data Lakes, next, covers the alternative storage model warehouses increasingly sit alongside rather than replace — and Lakehouse Table Formats covers how that boundary has been blurring.
